titulo: Development of a Drug Delivery System with Bacterial Cellulose and Gelatin: Physicochemical and Microbiological Evaluation
titulo_curto: A cellulose dressing that fights resistant bacteria

em_1_minuto.titulo: Bacteria that are more and more resistant
em_1_minuto.texto: According to the WHO, antibiotic resistance caused 1.27 million deaths in 2019. Wounds infected by resistant bacteria are hard to treat.

em_1_minuto.titulo: A dressing film with six ingredients
em_1_minuto.texto: They combined gelatin, cellulose produced by bacteria, sericin (a silk protein), citric acid, PEG 400 and nisin, a natural molecule that kills bacteria.

em_1_minuto.titulo: It worked even against hospital bacteria
em_1_minuto.texto: The film stopped the growth of all 7 bacteria tested, including 4 resistant ones from hospitals, and also showed antioxidant action.

em_1_minuto.titulo: A first step toward smart dressings
em_1_minuto.texto: This is an early lab study. Before reaching people, tests of the material's strength and safety are still needed.

secoes.lede: Antibiotics are losing strength, and infected wounds call for solutions that act locally for longer.

blocos.html:
Antimicrobial resistance happens when bacteria stop responding to the drugs that used to kill them. Overuse of antibiotics is the main driver of this problem. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, only about 8% of hospitalized patients had a bacterial infection, but approximately 75% received antibiotics.

Bacteria such as Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter are among the most worrying in hospitals.

Ointments and creams applied to the skin come off the wound easily. That is why there is growing interest in films and dressings made of natural polymers, which stay in place, protect the wound and release the drug gradually. The Uniso group has worked for years with bacterial cellulose, a very pure, strong material that the body tolerates well.

blocos.titulo: The film's six ingredients (and the role of each)

itens.texto: The base of the film. It fills the spaces between the cellulose fibers.
Provides structure and strength. It is produced by the bacterium Komagataeibacter xylinus.
Plasticizer: makes the film more flexible and keeps it from drying out.
Binds the film's molecules together and helps “open up” the protection of certain bacteria.
Silk protein. Adds elasticity and helps keep the film hydrated.
Natural peptide that kills bacteria. It is the dressing's “active ingredient”.

secoes.titulo: How the film was made and tested
secoes.lede: Everything was done in the lab, comparing the complete film with a “blank” film, without nisin or sericin.

itens.texto: The bacterium grew for 4 days at 30 °C in culture medium and formed membranes about 10 cm across. They were cleaned, washed to neutral pH and sterilized.

itens.titulo: Break down the cellulose with an enzyme
itens.texto: The cellulose was treated for 4 hours at 50 °C with cellulase, an enzyme that breaks up clumps. This way it spreads better in the film.
The gelatin was dissolved at 80 °C. After cooling to about 40 °C, it received the other ingredients, was poured into a dish and dried for 48 hours.
In 96-well plates, they tested the smallest amount of nisin and sericin able to stop bacterial growth (MIC).

itens.titulo: Place the film on the bacteria
itens.texto: Pieces of the film were placed on plates with 7 bacteria: 3 from a reference collection (ATCC) and 4 resistant ones isolated in a hospital. After 24 hours, they measured the growth-free area around it (the halo).
For 1 hour, they measured how much the film neutralizes free radicals (DPPH test) and examined its surface under an electron microscope at 20,000× magnification.

blocos.html: Student's t-test was used for statistical comparisons; differences with p < 0.05 were considered real. Tests were done in triplicate.

secoes.titulo: The film blocked all the bacteria tested
secoes.lede: Choose a bacterium and compare the complete film with the film without nisin and sericin.

parametros.leitura: Gram-positive bacterium, common in skin infections. Only the nisin film formed a halo.
The largest halo in the study. The film without nisin also acted a little, probably because of the citric acid.
Gram-negative bacterium very common in hospitals. Only the nisin film blocked it.
Antibiotic-resistant hospital bacterium. The complete film formed a halo of more than 18 mm.
The smallest halo among the bacteria tested, but the complete film still stopped growth around it.
Even the resistant version of P. aeruginosa was blocked by the nisin film.
The film without nisin had a small effect. The complete film had a halo more than 3 times larger.

blocos.nota: Halo = area around the film where bacteria did not grow (mean ± standard deviation, in millimeters). “Resistant” = bacterium isolated in a hospital. Value 0 = no halo. Data from Table 2 of the paper.

blocos.html: Nisin is the ingredient that kills the bacteria. On its own, it stopped the growth of S. aureus from 0.00125 mg/mL and of E. coli and P. aeruginosa from 0.0125 mg/mL. Sericin alone had no action against the bacteria.

itens.texto: Semi-rigid, translucent, odorless film with visible cellulose flakes: good features for use on the skin.
The complete film neutralized more and more free radicals over time, with a clear difference from 10 minutes on. The film without nisin barely reacted.
The gelatin covered the surface and the components blended into the matrix, with some clusters of nisin and sericin near the edges.

secoes.titulo: How nisin started beating Gram-negative bacteria
secoes.lede: On its own, nisin acts almost only against Gram-positive bacteria. In the film, it got a boost.

itens: Citric acid “grabs” the calcium and magnesium that hold together the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria
Nisin, which couldn't get through before, enters the bacterium
The bacterium is destroyed, including antibiotic-resistant ones

blocos.html:
Films made only of gelatin tend to be hard and brittle. Bacterial cellulose, with its nanofibers, made the material more cohesive and strong. Sericin added elasticity and helped prevent drying, and PEG 400 made the film more flexible.

A similar effect had already been described with nisin combined with EDTA, another substance that pulls calcium and magnesium from bacterial membranes.

The authors propose that the film overcomes resistance in three ways: it releases enough nisin to overwhelm the bacteria's defenses, penetrates the biofilm and keeps up continuous pressure, which makes escape through efflux pumps or mutations harder.

secoes.titulo: What the study allows us to say
secoes.lede: A promising material for infected wounds, still at the start of the road.

blocos.html: Combining natural biopolymers with nisin produced a stable, flexible film with action against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including resistant ones, and antioxidant action. Combining these two functions is useful in skin wounds, where infection and oxidative stress delay healing.

blocos.titulo: What is still missing, according to the authors themselves
itens: Better measure the film's mechanical properties (strength, elasticity).
Assess biocompatibility: whether the material is well tolerated by cells and tissues.
Run biological safety tests before any use in people.

glossario.def: When bacteria and other microbes stop responding to the drugs that used to eliminate them.
Natural peptide produced by milk bacteria, used as a preservative and able to kill other bacteria.
Pure cellulose made of nanofibers, produced by bacteria such as Komagataeibacter xylinus.
Protein that coats the silkworm's thread. It helps hydrate and adds elasticity.
Two large groups of bacteria. Gram-negatives have an extra outer membrane that makes them harder to reach.
Area around a material, on a plate with bacteria, where they could not grow. The larger it is, the stronger the action.
Minimum inhibitory concentration: the smallest amount of a substance that stops a bacterium from growing.
Stable free radical used to measure antioxidant action: the more it disappears, the more antioxidant the sample.
Scanning electron microscopy: shows the surface of a material at magnifications of thousands of times.
A substance that makes a material more flexible and less brittle.
When the drug leaves the material gradually, acting locally for longer.
Reference collection of microorganisms. “ATCC” bacteria are standardized so studies can be compared.
